extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in genre theory (literature, linguistics, rhetoric, composition)
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic summary of genre theory across literary studies, linguistics (SFL and ESP), and rhetorical genre studies (RGS), covering definitions, models, relationships among genres, conventions, evolution, and pedagogical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary conventions / Generic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions are usual indicators such as phrases, themes, quotations, or explanations that readers expect to find in a certain genre (for example, science fiction is expected to be set in the future and have technological advances; realism is expected to contain people who could pass as real).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions act as shared practices linking present and past writers; they are neither wholly arbitrary nor immutably fixed. Writers consult predecessors and may 'stretch the generic rules.' Conventions provide flexibility: they enable individual expression while constraining reader expectations. Example anti-pattern: ignoring conventions entirely so readers cannot integrate the new text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martinian genre model: staged, goal-oriented, social process
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres are defined as 'staged, goal-oriented, social process' — staged because they accomplish tasks requiring multiple steps; goal-oriented because users are motivated to complete stages; social because texts are addressed to specific audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or analyzing a work, consider its stages (sequencing of moves), its goals (what activity it accomplishes), and its social address (who the audience is). This model supports pedagogical approaches that teach genre structure to enable production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) approach
rubrics_metrics.description: SFL scholars believe that language structure is an integral part of a text's social context and function; contexts recur as 'situation types' and linguistic choices are made within a cultural 'network of meanings' (social semiotic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation/production should account for how linguistic choices enact social roles and ideology. Pedagogically, SFL emphasizes teaching basic genre structures and context to help students create culturally informed texts (Sydney School). Consider situation types and which linguistic resources the genre routinely deploys.

rubrics_metrics.name: English for Specific Purposes (ESP) genre analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: ESP focuses on specific genres within spheres of activity (e.g., medical profession) and uses genre analysis for applied ends; it identifies discourse elements such as register, formation of conceptual and genre structures, and modes of thought/action in a discourse community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For professional/academic genre production, evaluate register appropriateness, discipline-specific rhetorical moves, and micro-level genre conventions. ESP is targeted at university/graduate-level and helps non-native speakers use conventions in particular contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical Genre Studies (RGS): genre as typified social action
rubrics_metrics.description: RGS views genres as typified ways of responding to recurring social situations; the social action itself is the genre, not merely the document or text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a work by the social action it enacts (what recurring situation it responds to) and how it fits or transforms community practices. RGS emphasizes process, uptake, intertextuality, and the dynamic role genres play in organizing social activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical situation (Bitzer): exigence, audience, constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A rhetorical situation contains three components—exigence (an imperfection marked by urgency), audience, and constraints—and exhibits characteristics that call discourse into existence and shape appropriate responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or critiquing a genre piece, identify the exigence prompting discourse, the intended audience, and constraints (cultural, institutional, material). The page lists six characteristics of rhetorical situations: (1) situation calls rhetor to create discourse; (2) invites a response; (3) response must meet necessary requirements; (4) exigence located in reality; (5) situations have simple/complex structures; (6) after creation situations decline or persist. Use these to judge fit between response and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uptake (illocutionary response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uptake describes the ways genres interact and the illocutionary response elicited by particular situations; meaning depends on the ceremonial/contextual frame (Anne Freadman — tennis analogy: players exchange shots that have meaning only within the game).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate texts by how they anticipate and produce uptake from audiences and other genres. Consider ceremonials (contextual settings) that alter what counts as a meaningful response; failure to match uptake can render a text nonsensical in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality and citation as genre practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres (especially scientific) develop practices of intertextuality and citation that create collaborative relations and establish how knowledge should be formulated and evaluated (Bazerman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work situates itself appropriately within its intertextual network—does it cite predecessors, engage with disciplinary norms, and use citation practices that support uptake and credibility?

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre relationships: sets, systems, sequences, ecologies, colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars propose terms for how genres relate: 'genre sets' (genres produced by an individual actor), 'genre systems' (systematic unfolding of genres in an activity setting), 'genre sequences' (regularized series), 'genre ecologies' (open set of genre options), and 'genre colonies' (genres moving across domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis/production should consider the larger configuration of genres an actor inhabits: what other genres co-occur, how genres move between settings, and how sequences or systems shape expectations. Examples: courtroom activity system; Edison engaging with journalism, finance, patents, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres as social institutions / social cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres embody communities' knowledge and ways of acting; they function as knowledge foundations and navigation tools for social activity (Berkenkotter & Huckin; Fishelov).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a text by how well it enacts and transmits community-specific knowledge and practices. Consider whether it reproduces, challenges, or reshapes institutionalized ways of acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader expectations and the demand for innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers demand compliance with established conventions so they can integrate new texts, but they also expect manipulation of conventions so texts are not tedious repetition; writers are expected to carry conventions 'one step further.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good genre work balances conformity (so readers can understand) with innovation (to add value). Excessive conformity is boring; excessive deviation may confuse or alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre evolution and mechanisms of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres change, evolve, and decay; change is difficult because institutionalized conventions resist single-handed modification. Successful change often requires kairotic moments and adoption by other participants, aided by cultural capital, domain expertise, and agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting genre innovation, recognize constraints: institutional reinforcement, need for allies, timing (kairos), and credibility. Evaluate whether modifications are significant, persistent, and widely adopted to become lasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of genre taxonomy (classification limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres are mutable and evolving; very few works have all characteristics of a single genre and edges between genres fade into one another. Taxonomy methods include aesthetic, ritual, and ideological classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid taxonomic judgments; instead consider multiple classification criteria (aesthetic traits, ritual/contextual practices, marketing/ideological categorizations) and accept ambiguous or hybrid categorizations as normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions and limits of genre as meaning-making tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres provide shorthand communication, resonate with familiarity, and shift with public mores and the zeitgeist; however, genre classification can obscure individual merit and impose prejudicial value judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genre as a heuristic to interpret and produce texts but remain critical of applying genre-based value judgments. Example: the western's visual shorthand (black hat/white hat) conveys meaning because of genre history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metagenre and institutional guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Metagenre is 'situated language about situated language'—institutional guidelines function as metagenres that rule out or endorse kinds of expression and mediate local communicative practices (example: DSM standardizing psychiatric discourse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how higher-order documents (guidelines, policies) shape genre expectations and constrain/enabled authors. When producing texts, follow relevant metagenres to ensure uptake and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech genres (Bakhtin): rhetorical responsiveness and intertextual history
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech genres are patterns of language-in-context (oral and written), responsive to social/situational context and laden with intertextual history and ideology; utterances and types are 'drive belts' from social history to language history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider dialogic/heteroglossic factors: how utterances resonate with prior discourse, social roles, and ideological positions. Good genre use attends to this intertextual and dialogic layering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions as enabling rather than merely constraining
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions are not fixed procedures imposed from without but are 'constitutive and enabling'—they allow writers to preserve aspects of a genre while transforming others and enable individual expression via responsive negotiation with predecessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating creative work, look for how the author negotiates conventions: effective manipulation demonstrates both awareness of tradition and purposeful deviation to achieve new effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context, cultural ideology, and situation types (Halliday)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language choices are made within cultural ideologies and situation types; contexts in which texts are produced recur and constitute a culture's 'social semiotic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or design texts with sensitivity to cultural ideologies and recurring situation types; what linguistic resources the genre uses depends on these contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical implications: teaching genres to improve literacy and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching explicit genre structures (SFL/Sydney School, ESP) helps disadvantaged or non-native students grasp the system in which texts are created so they can produce similar texts; ESP focuses on professional/academic micro-genres, SFL on macro-level contexts for primary/secondary instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pedagogy, select genre instruction appropriate to learners' contexts and goals: SFL methods for broad literacy/contextual awareness; ESP methods for discipline-specific rhetorical moves and registers.
